changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
changes.change: For deals where the finance buyer won't meet vendors: before pricing goes out, offer a named step, a 'what your failed orders are worth' analysis built from the customer's own three-month declines export. Package the result as a one-page business case in finance language that the champion can hand to the CFO. Lead with the customer's own figure, not the third-party study.
changes.why: The champion asked for 'a one-page business case' to hand the CFO, our SE offered to value the failed orders from a three-month export, and the rep sent the deck and pricing proposal instead to a CFO he never met.

changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
changes.change: Swap the average uplift for a customer-specific statement in the buyer's own words: why 'the big baskets' fail at checkout, why 'the card says no', and what those 'orders dying at the last step' are worth, explained and valued from the customer's own dashboard.
changes.why: The average uplift slide is the generic material that went to the CFO, while what landed with the champion was the specific explanation of the declines, tied to her own number ('Her number. Off their own dashboard.'), and she describes the problem as 'orders dying at the last step' and 'the card says no', not as authorization rates.

changes.change: Proof point for deals against an incumbent that answers with a lower rate: never let a rate-only comparison stand. Give the controller a total-cost view with the rate, the gateway fee, the cost of chargeback handling, and the revenue lost to declines. Pair it with the line that a lower rate doesn't fix 'orders dying at the last step', so the page can't read as 'the same thing'.
changes.why: The bank came back with only 'a better rate', every email after that was the rate, and the CFO decided on a controller's one-pager showing 'Our rate, their rate, side by side'. That page read as 'the same thing', and even the rep concedes that matching the price would still have left 'same rate, so why move'.

changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
changes.change: When the buyer comes to us because orders are failing: open with why your biggest orders fail at checkout, and what that costs you in your own numbers. Hold the global-infrastructure line for later.
changes.why: The deal started with a specific money problem, 'one in twelve online orders was failing at the payment step, and it was worse on the big baskets', and the processor couldn't explain why. That is the opener this buyer responds to, not global reach.
